title: A grocery run, then breakfast by the water.
summary: A Saturday Hannaford stop during our off-season trip to Wells, Maine: Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and breakfast at a waterside picnic table.
search: The journal / Out & about / Maine Hannaford · Our off-season Wells tripA grocery run, then breakfast by the water.Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and a waterside picnic table. A simple Saturday breakfast idea from our Maine getaway, with a grocery stop James was very happy to make.October 18, 2026 · From the family notebook The makings of breakfast on our Wells trip, before we found our table by the water. The little storyBorrow the picnic ideaWhat we picked upShare the story On our trip to Wells, a quick Saturday morning stop at Hannaford became breakfast at a picnic table by the water. We had brought our own glasses and plates, so our grocery-store breakfast got a proper little table setting. I’ve loved Hannaford for years. I lived in Vermont for a long time, and it is one of those familiar places I’m always pleased to see when we’re away. I was hoping for my favorite butter rum muffins. They were sold out, which was a small disappointment, but we found plenty else to enjoy. We picked up assorted muffins, chocolate-frosted donuts, cold brew and Oakhurst eggnog. The eggnog added a Maine connection of its own: Oakhurst is a longtime Portland dairy. At our waterside table, we mixed eggnog into the cold brew and made our own eggnog coffee drinks. James had his eggnog on its own. It’s never off-season for eggnog. James had a good morning in the aisles, too. James loves grocery shopping. He was enjoying himself so much that other shoppers commented, and we proudly shared that he is often the grocery-store trip leader in his classroom. Shopping is one of his favorite things to do, and it was lovely to have a chance to tell people about that part of his school day. Then it was breakfast by the water: muffins, donuts, our little cold-brew experiment and time to sit together. We enjoyed it so much that we forgot to take a waterfront photo. The butter rum muffins can stay on the list for next time. Original editorial illustration, inspired by breakfast during our off-season Wells trip. A small idea to borrowBring the table setting. title: A date at the Gardner.
summary: A date at Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, with our own photograph, practical caregiver planning, admission savings and museum accessibility notes.
search: The journal / Family & caregivers Boston, Massachusetts · Time for two A date at the Gardner. A beautiful place, a little time together, and a photograph of just the two of us. There is room for this part of family life, too. October 16, 2026 · From our family album Time together ↓Making it possible ↓Plan your visit ↓ Just the two of us at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. There is a place in our family album for just the two of us. Here we are at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, tucked beside a stone column, with that extraordinary courtyard behind us. A little Boston date, worth keeping. So much of family life happens in conversation about what needs doing next. The calendar, the ride, the groceries, the things that need remembering. I like having a photograph that holds something else: us, together, somewhere beautiful. The Gardner makes a lovely setting for that sort of outing. The courtyard gives you something to pause over before you have made a single decision about which room to see. Its plant displays change through the seasons; the museum’s own courtyard guide is a good place to see what might be there on a future visit. A museum date can be wonderfully modest. Choose a few rooms. Point out a detail you like. Ask which painting your partner would take home if such things were permitted. Leave enough time to enjoy being there without making the entire collection an assignment. Time together belongs in the family calendar. Make the date small enough to happen. For parents and caregivers, getting out together can take real arranging. Reliable help, money and a workable window of time all matter. When those pieces are available, a short date deserves a place in the plan. An hour or two can be a perfectly good beginning. Before booking, agree who is covering care, the return time, and how to reach you if needed. Put the essential information in one place; our caregiver handover guide can help. Build in the journey home so the last room does not become a race against the clock. Choose one main stop and let anything else be optional. The museum lists Café G for food and coffee; check its arrangements separately if you want to add it. Leaving after the museum is also a complete date. And if a museum visit is beyond this week’s budget or support arrangements, keep the idea of time together in a smaller form: a cup of tea after the house settles, a shared album, a few minutes talking about something you are both looking forward to. The people doing the caring belong in the picture, too. The practical details left inBefore your own Boston date. Tickets, timing & a less expensive dateThe museum is at 25 Evans Way, Boston. Advance timed tickets are recommended. Standard adult admission is currently $25; ages 17 and under enter free. It is closed Tuesdays. Check current hours and availability on the official visit page.Thursday evenings are free, 5–9 p.m. Registration opens Tuesday at 10 a.m., two days beforehand; walk-up admission is not guaranteed. Use the Free Thursday Nights page to book. Participating library passes offer $5 admission for up to four adults; you must reserve the pass and obtain timed tickets with its code. A free evening may be busy, so choose the timing that suits you. Mobility, seating & sensory considerationsThe museum reports elevators in both buildings and a Palace lift to bypass the two steps before its main elevator. Free loan wheelchairs, rollators and canes are limited and first come, first served. Historic rooms have varied flooring, narrow doorways and low lighting; some power chairs may not fit every doorway.Gallery benches are available, with fewer on the upper Palace floors. Public restrooms have accessible stalls. These are the museum’s published provisions; we have not tested each route or facility. For individual access questions, call 617-278-5156 and review the accessibility guide. Ask about a quieter visiting time if crowds or sound affect your plans. Arrival & parkingThe museum has no dedicated visitor parking lot. Its directions page lists nearby options, including discounted Simmons garage parking with museum validation. The access guide lists two designated accessible spaces and a ramped loading zone outside the museum, plus four accessible spaces on Tetlow Street. Allow time for the trip between parking and the entrance. Check the official directions and parking information before setting out. If you are planning a later visit with the familyThis photograph is from our couple’s outing. A family visit can have its own pace and plan. Preview the museum’s visitor guidelines, keep communication supports available, and ask staff about any essential items or accommodations before arriving. A short visit with a clear ending is a useful starting point. Visitor information checked October 16, 2026 against the museum’s pages linked above. Hours, offers and arrangements can change. The photograph is from our own visit; the planning suggestions are for a future outing. title: Words matter. So does context.
summary: How An AUsome Life approaches autism, disability, high-support needs and respectful representation.
search: Editorial standardWords matter. So does context.An AUsome Life uses clear, respectful language and avoids turning disability into either tragedy or inspiration content.Identity-first by defaultWe usually use “autistic person” rather than “person with autism,” while respecting an individual’s own preference when known.High-support / profoundWe use high-support language when it helps explain access needs. “Profound autism” may appear when discussing the specific high-support experience this publication covers; we do not present the term as universally preferred or as a hierarchy of human value.No pity framingSupport needs can be significant without making a disabled person a tragedy, lesson or campaign prop.Age-respectful alwaysTeenagers remain teenagers. We do not infantilize someone because their communication, learning or daily-living support needs are substantial.For brandsWe will not use cure/fixing language, staged distress, forced participation or intimate private details to make a story more emotional. Product claims must stay within responsible evidence.
